title: Restriction on Entry of Certain Nonimmigrant Workers
summary:
The administration has issued a proclamation that temporarily restricts entry for new hires under the skilled worker visa program (commonly known as H‑1B) unless the sponsoring employer pays $100,000 per petition. The stated goal is to curb misuse of the program, raise wages, and prioritize higher-skilled, higher-paid roles.

For 12 months starting September 21, 2025, most employers seeking to bring in new skilled workers from abroad will face this added cost, unless the hire is deemed in the national interest. The measure applies to candidates currently outside the United States and is paired with directions to tighten against short-term business visitor visas being used as a workaround. The proclamation also instructs agencies to begin new rules to raise required wage levels and give priority to higher-paid, highly skilled applicants. The document cites increases in foreign participation in tech fields, reports of layoffs alongside visa approvals, and concerns about wage suppression and national security as reasons for the change.

Who is likely to benefit? American workers in computer and related fields—especially recent graduates and entry-level candidates—may see improved job prospects and potentially stronger wage growth if employers turn more to domestic hiring. Companies seeking truly specialized, top-tier talent may still proceed under the national interest exception or by absorbing the fee, and higher prevailing wage standards could help level competition across the market.

Who may be negatively affected? Employers that rely on recruiting from abroad, particularly for large-scale outsourcing or lower-cost staffing, will face higher costs and more scrutiny. Smaller firms and startups with limited budgets could find it harder to hire international candidates, even for niche roles. Prospective foreign workers waiting to start jobs in the United States may experience delays, uncertainty, or rescinded offers if employers choose not to pay the fee. Depending on how the rules are implemented and whether the policy is extended, teams that depend on international talent could see project slowdowns or talent gaps in the near term.
